paras: The shooting of Jesse Bagents was an ambush on the night of December 26, 1903, in which three white men fired a shotgun at Bagents, a Black man, and his younger brother on the Monticello road about four miles from Brookhaven, in Lincoln County, Mississippi. Bagents was hit in the back and left for dead, but the county coroner found him alive the next morning and judged him likely to recover. State papers counted the attack among the Lincoln County whitecap outrages, and a widely reprinted paragraph in January 1904 reported it as "another murder by whitecaps."

The shooting came while Mississippi papers were reporting a series of whitecap attacks in Lincoln, Franklin and Amite counties and while legislation to suppress the "whitecapper bands" was being debated.

According to the statements the brothers later gave, they were walking along the road about dark when they passed three men standing at the roadside, greeted them politely, and walked on. A few steps farther the men fired on them twice with a shotgun; Jesse fell and cried out that he was shot, while his brother ran into the woods. The Brandon News reported that "a dozen or more shots" were fired after the fleeing brother, who was not hit. Both brothers said the attackers were white men but that they recognized none of them.

The younger brother reached Brookhaven about 9 o'clock and reported to S. F. Magee and others that Jesse had been killed. Jesse had in fact got up after the attackers left and made his way to a sister's house nearby, and on Sunday morning he was taken by buggy to a cabin in the neighborhood.

On Sunday morning Coroner Lambright empaneled a jury and rode out to hold an inquest, but learned on arrival that the man was alive and found him in the cabin after a search through the woods. He had been shot from the rear, "freely peppered between the shoulders with No. 4 shot," and was expected to recover. No report of an arrest, an indictment or a later death was found in the coverage.

The Brookhaven Leader gave the fullest account under the headline "Negro Shot on the Monticello Road" and added its own inquiry into the victim's character. Citing Justice Hoffman, it called Bagents "an insolent and overbearing negro" who had earlier pleaded guilty to cursing a white man, Pink Jordan, in front of his wife and children. Such men, the paper wrote, "should be taught the lesson they deserve," but shooting them "in the back in the dark is not the right or manly way to do it."

Elsewhere in the state the shooting was read as whitecap work. The Brandon News printed the brother's first report under "Lincoln County Whitecaps Cause More Trouble," ending with his certainty that Jesse was dead. About three weeks later a paragraph headed "Another Whitecap Murder" appeared in the Oxford Eagle, and on January 23 in the Macon Beacon, the Grenada Sentinel and the Leader itself, describing Bagents as "ambushed and shot to death." That paragraph used the case to argue that new laws would fail while officers were "in secret sympathy with the lawless bands" and members of the law and order leagues also belonged to the whitecap organization.
No report of the shooting was found in the Black press.

Accounts differ on whether Bagents died. The Leader's report, based on the coroner's visit the morning after the shooting, found him alive and likely to recover, while the brother's first report and the January "whitecap murder" paragraph said he had been killed. The papers also place the shooting about four miles from Brookhaven, or five miles in the Brandon News.

reader.title: Shooting of Jesse Bagents
bases: Three white men ambushed and shot a Black man on a country road at night (A1, A2); the Brandon News and the syndicated 'Another Whitecap Murder' paragraph attributed it to the Lincoln County whitecaps (A2, A4), though the local Leader did not (A1).

Three unidentified white men shot Bagents without any authority (A1, A2), but the coroner found him alive and 'likely to recover' (A1); only the later syndicated paragraph says he was killed (A4). No pretext was stated by the attackers; the Leader's remarks on his 'insolent' reputation are the editor's, not a stated motive (A1). At most an attempted lynching.

The Leader and the Brandon News independently report the shooting of Jesse Bagents by three white men on the Monticello road (A1, A2); the outcome is contested, with the syndicated paragraph saying he was shot to death (A4) against the coroner's finding that he was alive (A1).
